newsitem.title: USA: Volunteers clean Philadelphia ave. in summit kickoff.
newsitem.headline: Volunteers clean Philadelphia ave. in summit kickoff.

text.p: Thousands of volunteers, including President Clinton and three former presidents, were poised to spruce up an eight-mile stretch of a Philadelphia street Sunday in launching a three-day "summit" to encourage volunteerism.

Clinton, retired Gen. Colin Powell, and former Presidents Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter and George Bush were to join sports and entertainment stars, corporate leaders and about 5,000 others to remove graffiti, clean up vacant lots and build a playground along the city's Germantown Ave.
"We're going to turn America on for the next three days by showing what we can do," Powell said here Saturday in preliminary festivities.

Sunday's events were to begin with a sunrise service at the site of a volunteer project to build an entire playground in one day. The event will be near the Marcus Foster sports stadium, site of a kickoff rally later Sunday morning.
Clinton, Powell, Bush, Carter and others were to address the rally, then join the other volunteers for an afternoon of cleanup work.

"Citizen service is neighbour helping neighbour," Clinton said in his weekly radio address Saturday. "It's part-time volunteers and full-time community service workers. It's communities coming together to solve common problems. And it is an essential part of what it means to be an American."

The summit aims to encourage more volunteerism in support of an estimated 15 million American children living in poverty, with a target of improving living conditions for 2 million of them by the year 2000.

This would require, on top of existing volunteer efforts, about 1 million Americans devoting an average of one day a week, said Terry Williams, a partner in McKinsey & Co., a consulting firm which prepared a study on economic aspects of the summit for its organisers.

An estimated 45 percent of Americans spend an average of five hours a week in volunteer service, he said. But he said efforts also need to be refocused to helping youths before they get in trouble. "Very little is going into this subject today," Williams told Reuters.

The study estimated that meeting the goals of the summit would cost roughly $15 billion and produce some $89 billion in benefits in reducing problems such as drug and alcohol abuse, failure to complete high school, crime and unemployment.

Stuart Shapiro, chief organiser of the summit, acknowledged that the goal of assisting 2 million children was modest in comparison with the number needing help. "It's a first step," he said. "It's an achievable goal."
